chapter_theme: Udayanan wins the king of Ujjain's trust by mastering the elephant, teaches Vasavadatta, is granted leave and an army, and flees with her by Yugi's fire-trick on the she-elephant, which dies and is reborn a god, then fends off the hunters and reaches Jayanti.

cast.role: the king of Vatsa, held at Ujjain, who tames the elephant and teaches Vasavadatta
the king of Ujjain, Vasavadatta's father (named by titles in these verses)
the king of Ujjain's daughter, Udayanan's pupil
Udayanan's minister who plans the escape
a lady who tells a dream in verse 102; identity not clear
the princes of Ujjain, the king's sons
the brahmins who fix the hour
the she-elephant on which they flee
Udayanan, Vasavadatta and their companions riding the she-elephant
the forest hunters who attack the fugitives

98.reading: The elephant kneels to Udayanan like sons long parted who come back and bow to their father's feet, and the great man, secure in his seat, takes up the goad in his big hand and drives it.
98.nuance: The simile of sons returning to a father makes the animal's submission an act of love, not of force; the verse does not say which elephant this is, nor how it was brought to kneel.
98.event: The elephant bows down to Udayanan, who mounts, steadies himself and takes the goad.

99.reading: Udayanan takes the gem, the lute and the striped rope that are held out, ties them on, rides the elephant along every street in circles, and the king who watches him is glad.
99.event: Udayanan, riding the elephant through the streets in circles, delights the king of Ujjain.

100.reading: The king of Ujjain gives a priceless pearl necklace, which the strong youth puts on, and he rides into the fort gate under the tiger banner like a roaring lion.
100.event: The king gives Udayanan a pearl necklace; Udayanan wears it and enters the fort on the elephant.

101.reading: At the king's word that it is enough, Udayanan raises his hand, braces his toes on the elephant's brow, and makes it give its legs; the king, pleased, embraces him.
101.nuance: The only words spoken are the king's brief 'enough', which ends the display.
101.event: At the king's command Udayanan makes the elephant kneel, and the king embraces him.

102.reading: The king calls Udayanan his son-in-law, speaks kindly, and as they sit in pleasure a lady tells of a dream and asks him to teach, whereupon the great man agrees to instruct.
102.nuance: மருமகன் may be a courtesy of the king's here and not a settled marriage; later verses still speak of Vasavadatta as a pupil.
102.event: The king calls Udayanan his son-in-law; a lady reports a dream and Udayanan agrees to teach.

103.reading: The king has weapons taught to all his sons, and has the slender-waisted Vasavadatta brought to learn the lute, and the lord is glad.
103.nuance: The verse does not say who teaches whom the lute; the sense follows the preceding verse where Udayanan agrees to instruct.
103.event: The king has his sons trained in arms and brings Vasavadatta to learn the lute from Udayanan.

104.reading: The young princes ask 'elder brother' Udayanan to watch their skill, and ride elephants, horses and chariots and show him their ways with sword and bow in order, which he watches.
104.event: The princes of Ujjain display their riding and weapon skills before Udayanan.

105.reading: Vasavadatta comes and bows to the king with her lute; hearing it falter, the great man is kind, saying the lady has all faultless arts, and she asks that the fault of imprisoning him not be counted.
105.nuance: Line 4 is the first mention in the chapter of Udayanan's imprisonment as a wrong to be forgiven, and who asks whom is not clear.
105.event: Vasavadatta bows to the king, and she speaks of the fault of Udayanan's imprisonment.

106.reading: The princes watch amazed while Udayanan, singing by the rules and drawing the strings short and long, makes the girls fall in a swoon on the golden floor, and the elephant-riding king rejoices.
106.nuance: Who plays the lute here is not named; the sense follows the lines 3 to 4 and the preceding performance.
106.event: Udayanan sings and plays; the women faint, and the king is pleased.

107.reading: The king takes the Vatsa lord's hand and speaks kindly, writes on a palm-leaf the royal marks of the Vatsa land, and tells him to go there; the brahmins name the next day as the hour.
107.nuance: The king here lets him go openly, yet verse 109 turns to Yugi's trick; the poem does not reconcile the two, and the last line is hard.
107.event: The king dismisses Udayanan to Vatsa with a written grant, and the brahmins fix the next day for departure.

108.reading: The king gives the young lord two thousand rutting elephants, four thousand jewelled golden chariots, a thousand war horses and a very large number of soldiers.
108.nuance: The numbers are as the lines print them; line 3 is dense and the horse count is read only roughly.
108.event: The king gives Udayanan a great army.

109.reading: Yugi, holding to his sworn vow, takes a trick and the guise of a fortune-telling woman, and tells the city in pleasant words to go and bathe in the water in order to ease the fear of the trembling beast.
109.nuance: Yugi's deceit is done to keep a vow, not for his own gain, and the poem does not blame it; the sense of line 3 is uncertain.
109.event: Yugi, disguised as a kuratti, sets a stratagem and tells the city to go bathing.

110.reading: The king, after consulting, goes with the city to the pool outside the old town to bathe; Udayanan stands on a good she-elephant, and Yugi has the town set alight.
110.event: The city goes to bathe; Yugi sets fire to Ujjain while Udayanan waits on the she-elephant.

111.reading: Frightened at the fire, the army goes off with the king; Vayantakan comes and tells Udayanan, who gladly lifts the king's daughter onto the she-elephant, and her friend Kanchanai mounts too.
111.nuance: Whether Vasavadatta goes willingly is not said; the verse says only that Udayanan 'gladly' lifts her.
111.event: The fire scatters the court; Udayanan seats Vasavadatta on the she-elephant and Kanchanai joins her.

112.reading: Vayantakan takes his lute and mounts the strong she-elephant, the lord speaks a mantra in her ear, and as they cross the Panchavanam forest the lord tells her to halt.
112.nuance: The mantra of line 2 is not named and its use here is as a charm for steadiness, not the dying mantra of verse 114.
112.event: Udayanan whispers a mantra to the she-elephant; Vayantakan rides; the elephant is made to stop.

113.reading: The lines hail a noble king and say that the elephant has crossed a great stretch of eight hundred bows' length of land, which the god gave, and as the prince goes on the elephant begins to waver.
113.nuance: The measure in lines 1 to 2 and the speech in lines 2 to 3 are hard, and the speaker is not named.
113.event: The prince rides on and the elephant begins to give way.

114.reading: Seeing the she-elephant sink, the riders get down troubled; she falls to the earth bleeding, and as the great mantra is spoken into her ear she joyfully becomes a god.
114.nuance: The verse says only 'mantra' and does not name the five-fold salutation by which Jain accounts of such a death are known.
114.event: The exhausted she-elephant falls and dies; the riders speak the mantra in her ear and she is reborn a god.

claims.claim: a dying creature that hears the sacred mantra is reborn as a god

115.reading: The lady gets down and walks toward the nearby ground, her feet, soft as cotton, blistered red like coral, her anklets silent in her weariness, and she goes holding her friend's shoulder.
115.event: Vasavadatta, footsore, walks on leaning on her friend's shoulder.

116.reading: Udayanan sees the lady's distress and the lotus pool in the grove; Vayantakan says he will come back with the four-fold army, the king tells him to go to the city, and he goes.
116.event: Vayantakan goes to bring the army while Udayanan stays with the weary Vasavadatta by the pool.

117.reading: At sunset Udayanan bids the lady sleep with her friend and stays awake through the night; at sunrise the hunters gather round them.
117.event: Udayanan keeps watch through the night; at dawn the hunters surround him.

118.reading: The hunters rain arrows on the generous lord, who wards them off with his bow and, as their cruel arrows keep falling, bends his great bow and answers with crescent arrows.
118.event: The hunters shoot at Udayanan; he defends himself and shoots back with crescent-headed arrows.

119.reading: Helpless, the hunters set fire to the wood; the king says he will give them wealth to live on, and Vayantakan arrives well turned out with five kinds of food and the four-fold army.
119.nuance: The offer to the hunters follows their defeat, so the gift is a settlement and not a ransom; whether they accept is not said here.
119.event: The hunters fire the forest; Udayanan promises them wealth; Vayantakan arrives with food and the army.

120.reading: They eat the food gladly and stay that day; next morning the king mounts the fine elephant, the lady rides a palanquin with the army about them, and they enter Jayanti where the king sits at ease.
120.event: The party eats, rests and travels on to the city of Jayanti.

links.note: Verse 105 shows Vasavadatta with the arts that verse 103 had her taught.
links.teaches: The lute lessons planned in one verse come out as proof of mastery in the next, so the teaching is shown as having worked.

links.note: The fire in the town carries out the trick Yugi sets in verse 109.
links.teaches: Yugi's disguised talk of bathing is only a lure; the fire that follows shows what the lure was for.

links.note: The hunters who gather at dawn in verse 117 have fired the wood by verse 119.
links.teaches: The ambush that begins with a surround is not ended by Udayanan's arrows alone; it ends when the hunters fail and Vayantakan comes.

links.note: Both poems show a young prince making a rutting elephant submit before the king.
links.teaches: Both minor epics test a hero's worth before a king by his mastery of an elephant, but here the man is a captive and the rider's skill earns him his captor's trust.

links.note: Both tell of an animal dying while a mantra is spoken to it so that it is reborn a god.
links.teaches: In the Cintamani the dog must consent and think on the words, while here the elephant is simply spoken to and the change is at once.

links.note: The goad in line 4 is the tool of the elephant keeper; Tirumular's goad is the five letters that rein the five elephants.
links.teaches: The goad that in one poem governs a real elephant becomes the word that governs the senses in the other.

gains.a: the taking of the goad gets an inner reading as discipline over a creature of great force
gains.b: the image of the goad gets a scene in which it is used on a real elephant that has bowed already

links.note: Yugi's deceit is for keeping a sworn vow; the couplet says wealth gained by deceit does not hold.
links.teaches: Deceit that serves a promise and not wealth is not judged by the couplet, which shows how far its warning reaches.

gains.a: the ruse gets a rule against which to see that its aim is a vow, not gain
gains.b: the couplet gets a case where deceit serves loyalty, which tests whether its warning covers it

links.note: Udayanan stands under a rain of arrows and answers with his bow; the couplet gives the bull elephant under a sheaf of arrows.
links.teaches: The couplet's elephant only stands firm; Udayanan stands firm and also shoots back, so endurance in the story includes acting.

gains.a: the defence gets a name for the quality shown, steadiness when things fall apart
gains.b: the couplet's image gets a man who stands and answers where the elephant only stands

links.note: Udayanan, a captive, rides in triumph on the elephant; the quatrain says kings who rode elephants fall when their deeds turn.
links.teaches: The story reverses the quatrain's fall, showing a captive king raised through skill and not through deeds, which limits how far the quatrain's warning is the whole account.

gains.a: the captive's triumph gets a reminder that a king's elephant-riding rank can be lost
gains.b: the quatrain gets a case in which a fallen man rises on an elephant by skill

source_issues: Verse 102: the speaker and identity of திருமகள் is not clear.
Verse 105 lines 3 to 4: the grammar is hard and who forgives whom is uncertain.
Verse 107 line 4 and verse 108 line 3 are hard to read.
Verse 113 lines 1 to 3: the measure and the speaker are not clear.
Verse 109 line 3 is hard to parse.
